section_summary: This section documents the internal organization, personnel, and budgetary concerns of the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Gaimusho) from 1932 to 1935. A prominent focus is the bureaucratic friction between moderate career diplomats, exemplified by Vice Minister Hachiro Arita, and assertive ultra-nationalist factions represented by Toshio Shiratori and Masayuki Tani, culminating in Arita's resignation and Shigemitsu's appointment alongside the reassignment of Shiratori. The section also includes extensive personnel and seniority rosters of the Japanese Foreign Office and diplomatic corps, plans for reorganizing regional bureaus and overseas posts, and comparative studies of U.S. and Japanese foreign service budgets.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of a seniority list of Japanese Foreign Office and diplomatic service officials.
subfiles.summary: Pages 81-85 conclude a personnel register ranking Japanese diplomatic officers and Foreign Office personnel by grade. The entries list names alongside their administrative and diplomatic ranks, ranging from secretaries and vice consuls to diplomatic attachés and interpreters.
subfiles.title: List of Japanese Foreign Office Officials (Continuation)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Count Uchida's formal installation as Foreign Minister and his press statements.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Count Yasuya Uchida was formally installed as Minister of Foreign Affairs on the morning of July 6, 1932. In an interview with Japanese pressmen, Uchida asserted that Japan's foreign policy would remain unchanged, claiming what is due while avoiding unnecessary conflict with other powers. Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori confirmed the accuracy of the remarks.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 187 from Tokyo regarding Installation of Foreign Minister Uchida

subfiles.about: State Department charge slip recording the withdrawal of file papers.
subfiles.summary: A standard Department of State charge slip recording the checkout of file numbers 894.021/28 and 29 on October 12, 1945.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.021/28-29

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a telegram from Peiping regarding Count Uchida.
subfiles.summary: Document file note indexing Telegram No. 771 from China concerning the arrival and installation of Count Uchida as Foreign Minister, filed under 793.94.Commission/292.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/30

subfiles.about: Telegram quoting Japanese press reports on Uchida's forthcoming foreign policy statements.
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson transmits a report from Nippon Dempo regarding Count Uchida's impending arrival in Tokyo and installation as Foreign Minister. The report forecasts Uchida's position to the League Commission, emphasizing Japan's support for Manchuria's self-determination, compatibility of Manchukuo's establishment with the Nine Power Pact, and Japan's stance as mediator in the Dairen customs dispute.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 771 from Peiping regarding Foreign Minister Uchida's Policy

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding statements by Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note pointing to Tokyo Despatch No. 69 filed under 894.00/428, concerning misleading press statements issued by Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/31

subfiles.about: Departmental routing memorandum forwarding Tokyo Despatch No. 307.
subfiles.summary: Internal State Department memorandum noting the receipt of Despatch No. 307 from Tokyo transmitting a translated list of Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service officials for reference purposes.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum regarding Tokyo Despatch No. 307

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting extensive rosters of Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service personnel.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits comprehensive registers of Japanese Foreign Office and Foreign Service personnel as of February 1, 1933. Enclosure 1 details departmental bureaus, sections, embassies, legations, and consulates worldwide, identifying ambassadors, ministers, section chiefs, and consular officers. Enclosure 2 arranges these officials hierarchically according to imperial civil service ranks (Shinnin, Chokunin, and Higher Civil Service grades 1 through 7).
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 307: Japanese Foreign Office Officials and Seniority Lists

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding a proposed Diplomatic Council in the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note to Tokyo Despatch No. 48 filed under 894.00 P.R./64, reporting that the Japanese Privy Council recommended establishing a Diplomatic Council in the Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/33

subfiles.about: Press clipping/report on the proposal to establish a Diplomatic Council.
subfiles.summary: Reports Japanese press accounts that the Privy Council suggested creating an advisory Diplomatic Council within the Foreign Office, modeled after the body that existed during the Terauchi administration in 1917.
subfiles.title: Report on Creation of Diplomatic Council in the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: State Department memoranda routing Tokyo Despatch No. 401 regarding personnel changes.
subfiles.summary: Internal memoranda from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs calling attention to Tokyo Despatch No. 401 concerning major staff shifts in the Japanese Foreign Office, including biographical notes on the new Vice Minister, Mamoru Shigemitsu.
subfiles.title: FE Memoranda regarding Personnel Changes in the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch analyzing the political conflict behind the resignation of Arita and removal of Shiratori.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed assessment of the resignation of Vice Minister Hachiro Arita and appointment of Mamoru Shigemitsu. Grew explains that Arita's departure was driven by friction between moderate career diplomats and the chauvinistic, military-backed faction led by Toshio Shiratori and Masayuki Tani. To prevent total extremist control and appease senior field diplomats, Foreign Minister Uchida orchestrated a compromise transferring Shiratori to Sweden and Tani to Manchukuo, which Grew anticipates may reduce abrasive anti-American rhetoric.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 401: Changes in Japanese Foreign Office Personnel

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding reasons for Arita's resignation and Shiratori's appointment.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet pointing to Tokyo Despatch No. 419 filed under 894.00 P.R./66, reviewing the circumstances of Arita's resignation and Shiratori's appointment as Minister to Sweden.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/35

subfiles.about: Excerpt from a periodic political report summarizing Foreign Office personnel changes and anti-British agitation.
subfiles.summary: An excerpt from a periodic political report discussing rising anti-British sentiment following the abrogation of the Indo-Japanese trade agreement. It also reviews the discord caused by Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori's aggressive press statements, culminating in Arita's resignation and Shiratori's assignment to Sweden.
subfiles.title: Periodic Report Excerpt: Important Changes in the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation with George Sokolsky regarding the removal of Shiratori.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck records a conversation with journalist George Sokolsky regarding the dismissal of Toshio Shiratori. Sokolsky reported that complaints from diplomats abroad, including Consul General Horinouchi in New York and Ambassador Debuchi, over Shiratori's abrasive style damaged U.S.-Japan relations. Statements made by Yosuke Matsuoka following his return from Geneva served as the final catalyst for Shiratori's transfer.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Stanley K. Hornbeck and George Sokolsky

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation with Japanese Embassy Attaché Eiji Wajima regarding Foreign Office politics.
subfiles.summary: Laurence Salisbury records an extensive discussion with Japanese Embassy Attaché Eiji Wajima regarding the bureaucratic rivalry between Arita and Shiratori. Wajima clarified that Masayuki Tani was opportunistic rather than a dedicated member of Shiratori's clique. Wajima predicted shifts in major diplomatic appointments, including the likely recall of Ambassador Debuchi, and anticipated continued moderate military dominance under leaders like General Masaki following General Araki's anticipated resignation. (Pages 138 and 140 contain duplicate versions of page 2).
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Laurence E. Salisbury and Eiji Wajima

subfiles.about: Report excerpts discussing proposed expansion of Japanese diplomatic missions and economic diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: Excerpts from Embassy reports examining the Foreign Minister's advocacy for expanding diplomatic and consular services under the rubric of 'economic diplomacy.' Despite general Cabinet budget opposition, the Foreign Office sought funds to establish new legations in Egypt, Abyssinia, Afghanistan, and Colombia, alongside additional commercial counselors and secretaries across Europe, Asia, and the Americas to support export trade.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpts: Contemplated Expansion of the Japanese Foreign Service

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding the establishment of a Trade Commission in the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note to Tokyo Despatch No. 481 filed under 600.9415/13, concerning the creation of a Trade Commission within the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/39

subfiles.about: Memorandum regarding the organization and staffing of the Foreign Office Bureau of Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck submits an excerpt describing the Bureau of Intelligence of the Japanese Foreign Office, comparing it to the State Department's Office of Current Information. The note highlights the bureau's rapid growth since 1920, its direct press contacts, and its employment of higher civil service officials, clerks, and distinguished journalists.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Bureau of Intelligence of the Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: State Department charge slips recording file checkouts.
subfiles.summary: Four Department of State charge slips recording the withdrawal and transfer of file numbers under 894.021 on October 12, 1945.
subfiles.title: Charge Slips for File 894.021

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding the split of the European-American Bureau.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note to Tokyo Despatch No. 788 filed under 894.00 P.R./77, regarding the Diet's approval to split the European-American Bureau into distinct European and American Bureaus under Shigenori Togo and Kensuke Horinouchi respectively.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.021/41

subfiles.about: Report excerpt regarding the creation of separate European and American Bureaus in the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Details the administrative division of the Foreign Office's European-American Bureau into two separate bodies following Diet budget approval. Kensuke Horinouchi was slated to head the new American Bureau, while Shigenori Togo was designated chief of the new European Bureau.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt: Creation of a Separate American Bureau in the Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum analyzing Japanese Foreign Office expenditures compared to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: An analytical memorandum detailing the Japanese Foreign Office budget for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1934, totaling approximately 26,400,000 yen (about $8,500,000 to $15,200,000 depending on exchange rates). It notes the surprise of Japanese officials upon discovering that U.S. State Department appropriations were comparatively modest given the size of the respective services.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum: Comparison of Foreign Office and State Department Appropriations

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting Japanese Foreign Office inquiries into U.S. State Department budget figures.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew recounts a conversation with diplomat Shunichi Kase, who revealed that the Japanese Foreign Office surveyed U.S. State Department budget figures hoping to justify its own requests for expansion, secret funds, and consulates. Japanese officials were incredulous at how low the U.S. appropriations were and initially suspected an error in the cabled data.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 854: Survey of State Department Appropriations by Japanese Foreign Office

subfiles.about: Instruction transmitting comparative budgetary data on American and Japanese Foreign Services.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo a comparative statement prepared by the Department of State detailing appropriations, salaries, and allowances for the American and Japanese foreign services.
subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo regarding Comparative Foreign Service Budget Figures

subfiles.about: Internal State Department note concerning a missing confidential seniority list.
subfiles.summary: A brief handwritten departmental note in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs remarking that the confidential 'Seniority List' was missing from the file.
subfiles.title: FE Note on Missing Confidential Seniority List
